London by-election spin cannot mask the crisis of accountability engulfing Westminster.
Back Zack or Sack?
Evidence: Progressive Electoral Breakthrough, Internal Crisis and Defeat, Leadership Self Preservation
#Aletheia #UKPol 🌐

Green Party leader Zack Polanski framed his Holborn and St Pancras loss as a historic breakthrough, claiming tripling the vote proves an expanding progressive movement ready to sweep Westminster.
Stated Judgement: (+0.70, +0.55) — Greater Good

In reality, Polanski lost by over 3,300 votes, merely absorbed preexisting leftist blocs, and faces party rebellion alongside an EHRC antisemitism probe, while Labour spins an eroded vote share as a triumph.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.78, -0.86) — Greater Evil

Verdict: FAIL — Fall into Destruction. Both parties replaced substantive democratic accountability with cynical public relations, hiding internal division behind manufactured optimism.
Integrity: Meaningful Distortion (Hypocrisy: 8.60, z: 3)

- Polanski: FAIL (-0.78, -0.86) — Spins defeat as a victory.
- Labour: COND (-0.65, -0.55) — Masks falling vote share.
- Playbook: COND (-0.40, 0.30) — Treats governance as PR.

Labour held Holborn and St Pancras with 45.2% of the vote under Andy Burnham, while Green leader Zack Polanski took second at 32.8% amid fierce internal party rows over his handling of antisemitism motions.

The Bright Side:
A 39% turnout in a safe seat proves voters refuse to rubber-stamp party spin. By rejecting entrenched tribalism, constituents force both leaderships to confront simmering rank-and-file policy revolts.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
This is a WHAT vs WHO error. The campaign claimed to empower local residents (WHO), but functioned solely to insulate party elites (WHAT). The bait was progressive governance; the switch was raw factional self-preservation.

Social Physics Analysis:
Polanski executed a classic selfish loop: hiding leadership vulnerability behind pretexts of structural growth, while projecting blame onto internal dissenters instead of resolving deep ethical fissures.

The Trajectory: The Path of Fall into Destruction.
When you map the gap between stated intentions and ground-level results, it plots a direct trajectory toward Greater Evil. High negative will and heavy moral contraction collapse hollow PR into systemic crisis.

The Unavoidable Truth: Losing an election while facing internal revolt is a defeat, not an expansion.

The Unavoidable Lie: Slogan-heavy broadcast rounds can substitute for resolving institutional antisemitism.

Alethekanon:
Electoral mathematics cannot be rewritten by morning broadcast spin. When vote share drops and regulatory complaints mount, treating collapse as victory signals deep institutional denial.

Awwthekanon:
Voters put their faith and energy into campaigns hoping for real community care, only to see their genuine hopes hijacked by party managers scrambling to save their own careers. People deserve real care, not spin.

Brothekanon:
Bro, you lost by over three thousand votes and your party icon is calling you out on live television. Claiming you crushed it while the coffee machine eats everyone's coins is next-level copium.

Spirithekanon:
"He who boasts of his achievements has no true merit; he who glorifies himself does not endure." Tao Te Ching 24 FAIL
When leaders substitute defensive spin for ethical ownership, they hollow out their movement from within.

By SAM FRANCIS

with MEGAN MCELROY and ISABEL LOUBSER

PRESENTED BY

Send tips here | Subscribe for free | Politics at Sam and Anne’s podcast | Listen to Playbook and view in your browser

Good Friday morning. This is Sam Francis, being escorted out of the Camden Council building as they turn the lights off, alongside Isabel Loubser.

HOLBORN AGAIN (SORT OF): And there we have it; Andy Burnham has passed his first major electoral test as prime minister. Labour holding on to a seat that has been red since its inception in 1983 should hardly be surprising, but it’s a sharp improvement given where the party stood nine months ago.

The biggest media focus this morning, however, is on Zack Polanski. The Green leader has just embarked on a red-eye tour of the broadcast studios, where he will inevitably have to make the case for himself to stay in post after a torrid few weeks inside the party. And he’ll face existential questions about whether the Greens are back to being a fringe outfit (rather than one that can sweep the board) in the Burnham era. Timings below, as ever.

Big disclaimer first: There is plenty from the Holborn and St Pancras by-election result that both Polanski and Labour can use to argue their case. The Greens tripled their vote from 2024, and more significantly, surpassed the combined 29.3% share that they and left-wing independent Andrew Feinstein won in the last election. That suggests Polanski has broadened that combined left bloc of voters, even if by a smidge since 2024 (he won 32.8% this time). Labour’s vote share dropped for the third successive election in the area, from 48.9% to 45.2% … but poll-watcher John Curtice noted on the BBC that Labour’s result was seven percentage points above its nadir at the May local elections. Turnout last night was 39%.

**A message from Lloyds Banking Group: Financial empowerment is taking shape differently across the UK. Nationally nearly nine in ten (88%) digital tool users engage with their finances digitally at least once a week. But what are they using those tools for? And what do those choices reveal about the financial priorities of people locally? Lives Empowered. A Nation Empowered.**

In other words: Let the spin wars begin. Green peer Jenny Jones is doing media too, while Labour Chair Bridget Phillipson is touring the studios for the victors. We may also hear from Burnham later, though the format was unclear as Playbook went to pixel.

Those results in full: Sagal Abdi-Wali (Labour) 12,292 (45.2%) … Zack Polanski (Green) 8,928 (32.8%) … Ewan Cameron (Conservative) 1,922 (7%) … Peter Newman (Reform UK) 1,612 (5.9%) … Patrick Stillman (Liberal Democrat) 924 (3.4%) … Tyler Johnson (Restore Britain) 692 (2.5%) … George Galloway (Workers Party of Britain) 314 … Briony Kapoor (Rejoin EU) 236 … Barmy Brunch (Official Monster Raving Loony) 87 … Helen Spiby-Vann (CPA) 63 … Clare Fischer (Climate) 51 … Ben Walker (UKIP) 51 … Ketankumar Pipaliya (Voice) 23 … Jonathan Silberman (Communist League) 9 … Tom Darwood (ND) 7.

GREEN EXPECTATIONS: The first sign Polanski would concede came in a gloomy statement at 10 p.m., saying “to be the main challenger shows how far the Greens have come.” More dollops of expectation management followed through the evening, with officials pointing reporters to the number of wards won and the party’s “highest ever vote share in a London constituency.” It wasn’t enough to take a seat where Labour had been confident of victory for weeks.

It’s Not Easy Being Green: Pressure was building on Polanski even as the votes were being counted. Green Party icon Caroline Lucas went on Newsnight to accuse him of failing to show leadership by staying away and not taking ownership of the “Zionism is racism” motion. Some Green members pushed back to Playbook, noting that Lucas still carries significant sway in the party — but did not use it to influence the vote.

Eek: Asked if Polanski should stand down, Lucas said: “I think let’s just see what happens in the coming days and weeks.” Those days and weeks have not got off to a good start.

Is the grass greener? “Of course I can carry on as leader of the Green Party,” Polanski told reporters. “Of course, I wanted to win. No-one runs an election to lose.” (Note the “can” there.) He told broadcasters in a pooled interview the Green movement is “so much bigger” than one election, adding: “We are going to build and we are going to grow.”

And TBF … from Playbook’s bleary-eyed view of the count in Camden, Polanski’s position looked secure. One official said that Green Party rules mean Polanski is safe from a coup, at least for another year when the leadership race is run again. Green Camden Councillor Hamza Chowdhury was slightly more enthusiastic, telling our Isabel Loubser: “This is a f*cking win mate. Labour might be celebrating now but wait till 2029 when we wipe the floor with them.”

However: The debate over what the Greens do now will be in full flow in WhatsApp groups this morning. No doubt some of those conversations will end up in the press soon enough. Noa Hoffman: your time is now.

More bad news for the Greens: The Campaign Against Antisemitism has reported the Green Party to the Equality and Human Rights Commission over its “Zionism is racism” motion because of what it called the policy’s “real potential to embolden expressions of antisemitism.”

Even more bad news for the Greens: The oat milk function on the coffee machine at the count malfunctioned — taking people’s money but producing no vegan-friendly cappuccinos.

NOW, TO LABOUR: Let’s zoom out a bit. Curtice told the Beeb overnight that the results show us that we’re “roughly where we thought we are.” Labour’s 3,364 majority shows it is enjoying a Burnham bounce — and has held together a coalition in London, after Burnham did so in Makerfield — but the party is still short of where it was in 2024, while the Greens have fallen back from their peak at the start of the year.

Don’t do it, Andy: The result should put to bed any discussions of a snap election, argued Curtice, since “this is not a result that is indicative of Labour being being able to do well enough to be able to win a general election with an overall majority.”

Strong message here: New Holborn and St Pancras MP Sagal Abdi-Wali gave what she called a “deeply personal” victory speech, celebrating the chance to represent “the place that gave me a home and my family a home, gave me opportunity and helped shape the person I am today.” Standing beside an increasingly stony-faced Restore candidate, Abdi-Wali told the room that “diversity is a strength” and warned: “We cannot allow that work built over generations to be casually undone by those who seek to divide us.”

There was some policy in there too, echoing several of Burnham’s greatest hits — ending homelessness, bringing water companies back under some kind of public control and creating better jobs. She then finished on a familiar note, with a near-carbon copy of the “Hope Again” messaging that ran through Labour conference. “Throughout our campaign, we chose hope, and the people of Holborn and St Pancras chose it with us,” she said.

Starm offensive: Abdi-Wali also paid tribute to the predecessors in her seat including the “late great Frank Dobson” and Keir Starmer, who she praised for “leading our party from opposition to government.” It raised a polite smattering of applause from the gathered Labour activists. Sadly Starmer did not turn up to the count, unlike at Makerfield, where Josh Simons was front and center to welcome his replacement.

MEET YOUR MP: Abdi-Wali, 42, has taken an unusual route to Westminster. Born in Somalia, she arrived in Britain as a child refugee and went on to become leader of Camden Council. She has also experienced hardship, choosing to support Tottenham Hotspur at a young age. Politically Abdi-Wali is firmly in Labour’s mainstream, backing Andy Burnham rather than Jeremy Corbyn for leader after she joined the party in 2015. She later chaired Starmer’s constituency party and remains a close ally of the ex-PM.

Green around the edges: Despite her centrist credentials, one of Abdi-Wali’s first acts as an MP could be to defy the prime minister if the government presses ahead with new North Sea drilling. There have been persistent rumors that a decision to approve new drilling near the Jackdaw gasfield was delayed to avoid Abid-Wali shedding votes to the Greens during the by-election. Asked by LBC this week whether she would support new licenses for the Jackdaw gas field, Abdi-Wali said: “I don’t think that this community would want something like that. So it would be something that would weigh up on my mind, definitely.”

PLANET TORY: Despite finishing a distant third, the Conservatives will take some comfort from holding their vote share, beating both Reform and Restore and keeping their deposit. That’s a better showing than recent polling might have suggested, given the Tories have been slipping nationally and were expected to trail Reform.

Kemi’s call reaction: A party organizer put some of the Tory performance down to Badenoch’s “powerful” conference speech attacking the politics of Reform and Restore. But the same official also credited Ewan Cameron with running a strong, locally focused campaign — “which some of the other parties can’t say.”

Spare a thought for the Lib Dems, who once again lost their deposit and got only a few hundred votes more than George Galloway, who didn’t even campaign due to his self-imposed exile in South Africa.

SCOOP — TECH BRO BURNHAM: The PM is planning to commit to a full or partial ban on “non-compete” clauses that are rife in high-flying tech and City workers’ employment contracts, six people with knowledge of the talks told POLITICO’s Dan Bloom, Joseph Bambridge and James Fitzgerald. Ministers think non-competes are a barrier to startups, even though they’re commonly unenforceable. An announcement is expected as soon as today — likely in a speech the PM is giving to a government-backed innovation summit from 10 a.m. The FT hears similar.

But but but … The government will stop short of defining the exact scope of a ban and any caveats will be worked out later, two of the people said. That’s despite Starmer’s government setting out options last November, which ranged from a total ban to restricting the clauses beyond a salary threshold or a set amount of time. This one could prompt a row: TheCityUK was among groups opposing a ban.

Windsor agreement: Downing Street says the speech in Manchester this morning will also announce £33 million to help recruit people for dementia trials, funding the BARBARA platform linking health data, researchers and clinical studies across the U.K. (and named after the late Barbara Windsor, who lived with dementia towards the end of her life).

Once again, there will be no Q&A after Burnham’s speech. But Downing Street has promised some form of media scrutiny — it just hasn’t said in what format yet.

GORDON’S ALIVE: Burnham’s will deliver his speech in Manchester alongside his old boss Gordon Brown, one of the key organizers of the Innovation Summit.

The dynamic could be interesting to watch. Beyond Brown’s official/made-up advisory role on global finance, the ex-PM has been unofficially advising many former protégés now at the top of the Burnham government — mostly through late night all-caps emails and phone calls.  Brown gave Burnham his first Cabinet roles as chief secretary to the Treasury then culture secretary, which exposed Burnham to the jeering of the Hillsborough survivors. That eventually shaped his view on Westminster politics.

In last month’s conference speech, Burnham said he is looking to emulate Brown’s  leadership in the wake of the global financial crisis and apply it to the current AI tech boom.

**What could the Warsaw Security Forum mean for Britain’s armed forces? Follow debates on NATO readiness, military capabilities and deterring Russia with Pro Morning Defense’s on-the-ground reporting. Sign up for a trial here. **

JENRICK ROLLS: Robert Jenrick gets Reform UK’s press conference podium back out of storage for a speech in London at 11 a.m., in which he’s expected to return fire on Kemi Badenoch, who spent the week calling him a “drama queen” and even unveiled a tapestry depicting him as some sort of tiny, crying goblin. According to previews in the Sun and the Telegraph, Jenrick will echo Labour’s attack that Badenoch is turning his old party into a “metropolitan pressure group for the wealthiest,” while claiming that “almost nobody outside of London and the southeast benefits from her tax policy.”

Questions, questions: Hacks will get the chance to quiz Jenrick after the speech for the first time since the wake of the Reform conference, and there’s lots of ground to cover. Starting from Reform’s poor performance in yet another by-election … the sanctity of Reform’s internal review, which cleared two senior aides who were caught in an undercover donations sting …  and whether Jenrick talked to Zia Yusuf before straying into his brief by restarting his vigilante journalism videos accosting shoplifters in Brixton.

He might also be asked about Caroline Wheeler and Kitty Donaldson’s report in the i Paper that a parliamentary investigation into whether Nigel Farage properly handled a £5 million gift from crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne is expected to report “within days.”

Don’t make any Christmas plans just yet: Reform doesn’t appear to be expecting good news. Officials are preparing for the possibility of another by-election before Christmas, with one senior party source telling the i Paper: “We will be ready.”

NAME CHECKED: The i Paper’s Wheeler has revealed that Kemi Badenoch and other senior Tory figures, including Tom Tugendhat and Priti Patel, were among more than 100 high-profile figures named in a dossier discovered at the home of the man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe. The newspaper reports that the dossier also contains the names of senior Reform figures, as well as former Labour MP turned independent Rosie Duffield.

Court circular: The man in question, Joshua Kerry, has also been charged with planning acts of terrorism. He is due to attend the Old Bailey for a preliminary hearing.

SCOOP — ONE DOWN: An agreement on linking the U.K. and EU carbon emissions trading systems is basically done, four people tell my colleagues Jon Stone and Dan Bloom. A deal is set to be unveiled at the U.K.– EU summit, penciled for Nov. 20. It’ll exempt companies from both sides of the channel from CBAM carbon taxes, but could raise the U.K. carbon price in the short term. Both sides are now just “tying a ribbon,” says one diplomat, although the deal won’t see the light of day without parallel deals on agriculture trade and youth visas, which are tricker.

BASE-IC INSTINCT: Despite all the recent arrests, U.K. military bases remain secure, Chief of the Defence Staff Richard Knighton has said. His comments, written up by the Times, came just hours after two Latvians were arrested on suspicion of a national security offense over an alleged break-in at an RAF base in Cambridgeshire used by U.S. and NATO intelligence personnel.

TROUBLING NEWS: Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant says a major package of amendments to the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill will arrive on Monday, including an explicit “no equivalence” clause covering British forces and terrorist acts. Bryant told the Independent’s “SAS: The Shadow War” podcast that a “big package of amendments” would answer “every one of the key questions” raised with ministers.

HEALTH CHECK: Peter Fonagy’s review of ADHD, autism and mental health has splashed the front of the Times, the Guardian and the Daily Mail — an unusually broad consensus that ministers have a problem on their hands. Each paper obviously has its own take, but the review warns of a risk of overdiagnosis of ADHD and autism, while saying the NHS in England is heading towards a “world of system failures,” with relentlessly rising demand for mental health support leaving patients struggling to get help.

WHAT THE GOVERNMENT WANTS TO TALK ABOUT: The Department for Education has polled teenagers and found 84% support more hands-on learning — which is a fortunate coincidence, given the government’s recently announced plans for vocational GCSEs.

COSTLY MISTAKE: Kemi Badenoch’s flagship party conference policy document overestimated the cost of net zero by nearly £500 billion, after apparently double-counting figures from the Climate Change Committee. The error, spotted by Carbon Brief and reported by the Guardian’s Peter Walker, saw the Tories put the cost at £957 billion when the actual figure was £478 billion.

NINE LIVES: Larry the Cat is back roaming the corridors of power after being rushed to the vet to have a cyst removed earlier this week, LBC’s Natasha Clark reports. The chief mouser had an operation but is said to be “recovering well.”

NO PAL OF MINE: Tom Watson says he doesn’t “agree with a lot of things” Peter Thiel says, despite now working at Palantir. Thiel has recently intensified his repeated warnings about the Antichrist blocking technological progress, attacking Barack Obama and Pope Leo XIV for their criticism of AI. Watson told the BBC’s Political Thinking with Nick Robinson that Palantir embraces a “pluralism” of views — including his own democratic socialist ones. But on calls to strip Palantir out of state contracts, he added: “Do you want the rule of law to lead procurement practice, or do you want mob rule to lead procurement practice?

REPORTS OUT TODAY: Deliveroo is calling on the government to ban unsafe modified e-bikes.

KENT CLEANUP: An illegal waste site in Kent has been cleared after 15 months at a cost of £15 million to taxpayers. Criminals had targeted the area at Hoads Wood, near Ashford, in 2023, dumping nearly 40,000 tons of waste over six months. It was the first waste “supersite” in England to receive central government money for the cleanup. The BBC has a write-up.

REVOLVING DOOR: The Times has quite the early-release story … A man who praised Andy Burnham as he walked out of prison under the government’s scheme last week, having served 78 days for breaching a suspended sentence for shoplifting, has been sent back to jail after going on a shoplifting spree that tied up police for an entire day.

LETTER OF THE LAW: A DUP MLA has claimed there is a “clear precedent” for criminal proceedings over the protests on the Garvaghy Road, according to the Belfast Telegraph. The Police Service of Northern Ireland has begun writing to people suspected of committing offenses during the protests. Sinn Féin said a number of its representatives and party members have received letters.

AIR STRIKE: Yemen’s Houthi rebels have reportedly destroyed an aircraft belonging to Saudi Arabia’s national carrier in a strike on Riyadh’s main airport, per the Telegraph.

MIAMI TALKS: U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will meet Ukrainian representatives in Miami today, Reuters and others report, with sources saying the discussions will focus on new ideas and ways to come up with a unified proposal to end the war. Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has confirmed the meeting, saying he was also counting on a European team to join his negotiating group.

ACCESS DENIED: The Trump administration is suspending Microsoft and several other companies from a program allowing foreign workers to apply for green cards. Vice President JD Vance accused the company of using the program to commit fraud.

**A message from Lloyds Banking Group:Across the UK, digital tool users in different regions are finding their own routes to financial empowerment.Yorkshire and the Humber is the UK’s digital budgeting hotspot: nearly half (44%) use digital tools to budget and track spending. In the East Midlands, one in four (24%) say digital tools have helped them pay off debt.Wales leads the UK among those who use digital tools to manage or grow investments, pensions or ISAs (23%). Northern Ireland’s ambitions are more future-focused: 17% say saving for education or training is a top goal—the highest share in the UK—signalling an untapped digital ambition.And half of Londoners (49%) report using AI for personal finance at least weekly, reporting average savings of £562 after following AI-powered recommendations—41% above the UK average.Read Money mapped by Lloyds Banking Group to see how local priorities are shaping financial empowerment across the UK. Lives Empowered. A Nation Empowered.**

Minister for Women and Equalities Bridget Phillipson broadcast round: Times Radio (7.05 a.m.) … Sky Mornings (7.15 a.m.) … BBC Breakfast (7.30 a.m.) … LBC (7.50 a.m.) … 5 Live (8.05 a.m.) … Today (8.30 a.m.) … Good Morning Britain (8.45 a.m.) … GB News (9.05 a.m.).

JOB NEWS: Miatta Fahnbulleh’s team has hired a raft of policy advisors. Ex-director for economic policy at IPPR George Dibb will lead on reindustrialization and jobs, alongside former Octopus Energy director Arthur Downing, who will lead on energy market reform and public control. Anne-Marie Philip Howell stays on at the team to do strategic comms.

SPOTTED … enjoying the fizz on Pall Mall at the launch of Andrew Roberts’ book “Napoleon and his Marshals: Victory, Rivalry, Betrayal”: Palantir UK CEO Louis Mosley … Deputy Conservative Leader Alex Burghart … former No. 10 Policy Director Munira Mirza … Tory peers Ed Vaizey and Lucy Neville-Rolfe … historians John Bew and David Starkey … adviser Sophie Jarvis … LOTO Head of Engagement Daniel El-Gamry … former peer Matt Ridley … and journalists Will Moore and Poppy Coburn.

SOUR TASTE: Outgoing IEA economist Chris Snowdon has hit back at Popbitch after a not-so-flattering write-up of the organization’s party at Conservative conference. In response to accusations that the think tank failed to provide Champagne after it was promised and hid private bottles of stuff nicer than budget Chardonnay for the staff, he posted on X: “We never said it was a champagne reception and the staff were drinking the same two-for-a-tenner dreck as everyone else.”

FRIDAY’S POD PICK: The Lib Dems have gotten round to promoting their “Conference Conversations” podcast (three weeks after the main event). You can relive it in all its glory here; it includes interviews with Ed Davey, Munira Wilson, Caroline Voaden and Sky’s Lucy McDaid.
